speechtext: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT NOT INTERVENE TO REVERSE CRTC DECISION ORDERING REIMBURSEMENT™ BELL CANADA SUBSCRIBERS

Mr. Speaker, Canadians were glad to hear about the CRTC ruling granting a refund to Bell Canada subscribers. According to the ruling, subscribers will be entitled to a credit amounting to about two months' service charges and long distance rates will be rolled back by roughly 20 per cent. The CRTC also ordered Bell Canada to provide telephone service to customers with hearing impairment in Quebec and Ontario.
This hard-earned victory is due to the 300-odd interest groups from all walks of life which appeared as witnesses during last summer's public hearings.
On behalf of Canadian consumers, I urge the Government not to intervene to reverse the CRTC decision.

CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION DECISION REQUIRING BELL CANADA TO MAKE REFUNDS TO SUBSCRIBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, consumer power and complicated hearings have paid off. Yesterday the CRTC announced a decision requiring Bell Canada to refund $200 million to telephone subscribers in Ontario and Quebec as a result of excessive revenues Bell had obtained. In addition, Bell has been directed to reduce rates for long distance calling by 20 per cent effective January 1.
This is welcome news indeed and marks the first time the CRTC has been as tough as this in any decision. I applaud the CRTC as well in its direction to Bell to provide a message relay service for the hearing impaired that will operate 24 hours a day. People with hearing handicaps have been lobbying for this for 10 years.
A monopoly such as Bell has an obligation to provide services at a reasonable cost. It is the job of the CRTC to see that returns are reasonable and that consumers are well served. The decision of the CRTC yesterday shows that the system can work.

subsubtopic: NONPAYMENT OF INCOME TAX BY TRANSCANADA PIPELINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the need for a fair, just, and equitable tax system for all Canadians, I wish to announce today's winner of the great untaxed corporation award. It is TransCanada PipeLines, which was, through successive Liberal and Conservative tax measures, granted the right to pay no taxes in both 1980 and 1981 on profits totalling $256.6 million.
Had the tax system been fair and equitable, and had TransCanada PipeLines been required to pay even a 25 per cent tax rate on its profits, average Canadians would have paid $64.2 million less in tax because of this one company alone.
This award is a reminder to the Government that there is a serious and immediate need for comprehensive tax reform.

subsubtopic: NEW IMPORT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion announced the Government's new policy on textile and clothing imports. This means the multifibre agreement under the GATT is renewed, and this Conservative Government intends to renegotiate and extend bilateral restrictive arrangements with more than 25 countries exporting low-cost clothing. Thanks to this new step, there will be a more moderate rate of growth of imports consistent with the domestic market. Those are two vital industries, employing as they do more than 20 per cent of Quebec's manufacturing manpower.
Further, the new policy includes a customs duty return program aimed at increasing the competitivity of our shirt

October 15, 1986

manufacturers, and the strengthening of border checks by laboratory analysis of the fibre contents of imported goods, as well as the review of the regulations dealing with the indication of the country of origin.
Those measures will ensure that a viable level of textile and clothing production is maintained in Canada and in my constituency, where the industry employs more than 5,000 workers.

subsubtopic: FARM DEBT REVIEW BOARDS-DELAY IN HEARING APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the farm debt crisis is getting worse every day with thousands of farmers across Canada facing the loss of their farms. In Ontario over 900 farmers are two to three years behind on their FCC loan payments.
Last June, in two sittings of the House, we passed the legislation creating Farm Debt Review Boards. Still, the Farm Debt Review Boards are not functioning in Ontario. Only three of the ten member board have been appointed so far. Over 100 farmers have applied for help from the board, yet not a single case has been heard.
Last Friday the Ontario Federation of Agriculture sent an urgent telegram to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) urging action by the Government, and cautioning the Government that farmers' patience is running out and they are becoming increasingly angry.
I call on the Government to take action and get these boards operating immediately. The Government must change its ways and give the farm debt crisis the urgent priority it deserves.

subsubtopic: EARLY PAYMENT OF CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, about
725,000	Canadian families, or 1.3 million children, will benefit from an early payment of the child tax credit this November, 1986. This credit introduced by this Government will provide timely assistance to Canadian families, and will reduce the need for tax refund discounting.
The prepayment, which is $300 per child, is an amount equal to approximately two-thirds of the full credit. The remaining amount, if any, will be paid after the 1986 tax return is filed in early 1987. The prepayment will automatically be made available to eligible claimants who had a family
income of less than $15,000 in 1985. Other recipients will receive their credit in the spring, as has been the case in the past. Furthermore, no applications for the prepayment will be required. This measure complements the $70 increase in the tax credit this year, and the measures to control the money that may be taken by tax rebate discounters.
By providing, for the first time, an early payment of the child tax credit, the Government is clearly demonstrating its concern for the needs of middle and low-income families in Canada.

subsubtopic: AWARD WON BY PROFESSOR JOHN POLANYI, UNIVERSITY OF TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to congratulate, on behalf of all Canadians, Dr. John C. Polanyi of the University of Toronto, who today has been awarded the Nobel Prize for chemistry for his work on the dynamics of chemical elementary processes.
Dr. Polanyi is the second Nobel Prize winner in chemistry in Canada, and follows the prize awarded to Dr. Gerhard Herzberg of Ottawa. Both men have had associations with the federal National Research Council, Dr. Polanyi as a postdoctoral fellow and Dr. Herzberg in a life-long career there.
In congratulating these men on their achievements, we must also reflect on the Black Wednesday that struck the NRC today in the budget cuts which eliminated 200 jobs, wiped out programs, and cut back the Herzberg Institute of Astrophysics.
Can we not better honour the persons who have brought recognition to Canada by strengthening our commitment to basic research instead of thoughtlessly disbanding the hard work of many talented scientists?

subsubtopic: NEED FOR FEDERAL REGULATORY REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recent takeover of the Continental Bank by foreign-owned Lloyds Bank was another signal to Canadians that the Government has not yet made good on its promise to enact comprehensive regulatory reform for the financial services industry.
The Speech from the Throne in 1984 contained a promise to follow through on the reform process begun under the previous Liberal Government. However, since then trust companies have failed, banks have closed their doors, and major financial institutions have come under the control of a non-financial institution. Studies and reports have proliferated. Provincial Governments are pursuing their own reform agendas, but our federal regulatory environment is virtually unchanged and the Speech from the Throne merely reiterated a two year old promise.
The Government is fast running out of time and options. Unless it replaces promises with action now, it will continue to be overtaken by events.

LABOUR, EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION NINTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-FAMILY REUNIFICATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to present to the House and to the Canadian public the Government's response to the Ninth Report of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration on family reunification.
At the suggestion of the Government, the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration examined ways to speed up processing of family class applications. I would like to commend the excellent work done by the committee and particularly the collective effort that has been shown by Members of Parliament from all three Parties under the distinguished leadership of the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes). The members participated in well over 100 committee meetings. Three full weeks were taken up in visiting immigration centres in Canada and posts abroad, as well as holding meetings with both immigration officers and potential and recent immigrants. The members received a clear feeling and understanding of those areas where the quality of service had not been acceptable.
I would like to reflect particularly on the quality of the report. The committee has provided me with a series of recommendations on how to provide service that is quicker, more courteous, fairer and, especially, more humane. I believe that a new era has begun for sponsors and for their relatives. Emphasis has been placed on improved training for immigration officers and an attempt is being made to provide services in the language of a client's choice. The Government understands the frustrations that have been felt by those who have participated in our immigration process. With our response, we are prepared to do something about those frustrations. Recommendations 5 to 10, which involve the creation of new categories of assisted family members, are perhaps the most exciting and far-reaching recommendations.
Unfortunately, because the House of Commons rules require a response within 120 days, there has not been sufficient time to consult with the provinces and the private sector organizations, which is necessary before developing the details of a major change of this kind. Those discussions have begun, and hopefully they can be brought to a successful conclusion. Most of the other recommendations have either been previously implemented, or are in the process of being implemented.
October 15, 1986



Through its response, the Government will be providing improved service in Canada for sponsors of immigrants belonging to the family group. From now on, it will be easier to complete a sponsorship application form because the people concerned will be encouraged to complete those forms themselves. The waiting period for an interview for sponsorship purposes will be greatly reduced. Moreover, a better service will be made available to immigrants abroad following a more efficient control of records as well as improved medical procedures.
If the time allows it, early in the New Year, I hope the Committee will be anxious to review the progress made as a result of our response.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I am pleased to have the opportunity so early in my term of office to table in this House a paper indicating not only the commitment of this Governement to improve the quality of life but also the result of a fruitful dialogue between members of all parties in this House.

subtopic: LABOUR, EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION NINTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-FAMILY REUNIFICATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the critic for my Party on immigration matters, and as a member of the Standing Committee, I am pleased to respond to the Minister. Let me say at the outset that I commend the Minister for at least having the detailed analysis on a recommendation by recommendation basis. That is certainly something that lacked such detail under his predecessor. However, I do not think that the ambitious remarks noted by the Minister will be translated into the affirmative responses to the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration.
It should be well noted that the stimulus for the committee report came from that most frustrating aspect of immigration practices and regulations in this country, as articulated by Members from all sides of the House, namely that Canadians were unsuccessfully able to sponsor their relatives, or if they were, there were great delays in the system, in some cases as long as two, three, and even four years. We have individual cases that go undocumented and unresponded to by our immigration officials abroad for up to periods of one year. Therefore, the question before the committee was how do we enable the system to facilitate the requests generated from Canadians here in Canada for the successful application of their relatives and loved ones throughout the world?
On the basis of the three corner-stones of the recommendations, the Minister has failed to adopt those recommendations as outlined by the committee.
First, the recommendations of the committee said basically that if we are to speed up the system in relation to family assistance applications there has to be a reallocation and a redesign of the classifications into priorities. The first priority is spouses and dependants; the second is parents with dependants, siblings and non-dependent children, as well as people who wish to adopt children who have been left homeless and
Statements by Ministers
without parents. Therefore, we gave a priority listing that would ensure that the immigration officials processed applications on a priority by priority basis relating to those classifications. I regret that the Minister has not chosen to embrace that recommendation.
As well, we suggested that points should be increased to those immigrants who have family members in Canada. We said basically in our report that if we are to take seriously the fact that an immigrant, or potential immigrant, has family in Canada, then we should elevate that consideration to the same points level as education, or having a job. Let us admit that having family members in Canada counts culturally, socially, and financially, and that such a person coming to Canada can expect support financially, culturally, and socially. Therefore, the Canadian state would not have to provide those services. The Minister, once again, did not accept our recommendation of giving additional points to those people.
The second recommendation was to shift resources throughout the world in relation to demand, and how that is being triggered in this country. That is to say, there are more demands being placed on the system in India and Hong Kong today than there are in Great Britain, yet there are more resources in the more traditional parts of the world. The Minister and the Government know that you control the flow of immigrants and the number of applications by the number of resources provided.

Although it is a timely report, and although he covers a good deal of ground in a very encouraging way, there are four serious gaps in his report. Some of them have alrerady been touched upon. I want to point out that in his failure to give any

support to the idea of improving family reunification immigration, as suggested in recommendations 5 to 10, the Minister suggests that the new point system will allow for perhaps half of what might be asked for by the relatives. He does not say that exactly, but that is what he implies. The facts are the opposite, and the Minister should know that between 1982 and 1985 both family class and assisted class immigration declined. In 1986, if we project from the first half of the year, it will have declined more disastrously than in the years before. The new point system is a failure from the point of view of family reunification.
Secondly, Minister suggests that there might be some meetings between the Health and Welfare officials and Immigration officials, and the committee. In fact, that is only an extension of the stonewalling that Health and Welfare did for six months, from January to June. While we were studying the report that Parliament asked us to study, Health and Welfare refused, even at the request of the Chairman, to allow us access to the manual which provides the rules under which Health and Welfare have increasingly over the last few years rejected family members and assisted relatives. In fact, the Government itself in the spring in its report towards equality, page 28, tells the public that that manual is available on request. That is false. The manual was not available to the committee during that six months of study. The promise of consultation carries no conviction whatever on the part of those of us who have experience.
On the matter of the posts abroad, it is patently obvious that what the Minister says in reply to Recommendation 48 is not in accordance with the facts. The resources are not distributed according to the volume of applications, successful or unsuccessful. The refusal of the bureaucrats to budge from the positions they have adopted in the past several generations is the main hindrance to family reunification at present.
Finally, on the matter of the entrepreneurs, it is a fact, as was pointed out and reported by my colleague months ago to the committee, to the benefit of the Minister and his predecessor, that staff has been transferred. Notwithstanding all the remarks the Minister makes about priorities being observed according to statute, staff has been transferred away from family reunification. It is a fact that entrepreneurial applications take several times as much staff time as family applications do normally. He can pick one example here and one example there to match them off, but he knows that he is twisting the story by hair-splitting and by doing that. In fact entrepreneurs by definition, having hundreds of thousands of dollars and being business people, are accustomed to paying for the service they get, such as for a visa, while families, being mostly poor, cannot.
